title: Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.
gist: Amazon tutorial on profiling PyTorch workloads on AWS Trainium via the TorchNeuron backend, using torch.profiler and Neuron Explorer. For RMSNorm, a naive eager implementation uses 2,355 microseconds of Neuron device time across 6 operator calls, versus 403 microseconds for torch.rms_norm and 376 microseconds for torch.compile, each a single fused dispatch.

insights.claim: AWS Trainium is a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference, and TorchNeuron is its open source native PyTorch backend supporting eager execution, torch.compile and standard PyTorch APIs with minimal code changes.
insights.speaker: Josh Longenecker
insights.so_what: Native PyTorch support lowers migration cost from NVIDIA GPUs to Trainium.
insights.quote: TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes.

insights.claim: TorchNeuron integrates with the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware.
insights.speaker: Josh Longenecker
insights.so_what: NKI is the escape hatch for hand-tuned kernels, analogous to custom CUDA work.
insights.quote: TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware.

insights.claim: The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point, which lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda, via the torch_neuronx package.
insights.speaker: Josh Longenecker
insights.so_what: Upstream-sanctioned extension mechanism makes the backend more maintainable than a fork.
insights.quote: The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point.

insights.claim: Profiling a Neuron workload uses NeuronConfig to choose data streams and NeuronCores and NeuronProfiler to export traces, passing ProfilerActivity.PrivateUse1 to torch.profiler and setting correlate_device_time=True so the key_averages() table shows Neuron device time.
insights.speaker: Josh Longenecker
insights.so_what: A practical recipe for getting device-level timing out of Trainium.
insights.quote: Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table

insights.claim: Without calling torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.
insights.speaker: Josh Longenecker
insights.so_what: A common pitfall that produces misleading blank profiles.
insights.quote: Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

insights.claim: Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for system trace, device timeline and per-engine breakdown, and profiles use paired .neff (compiled executable) and .ntff (hardware instruction trace) files sharing a numeric hash.
insights.speaker: Josh Longenecker
insights.so_what: Profiling tooling maturity is relevant to Trainium's developer experience versus GPU profilers.
insights.quote: Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown.

insights.claim: In Neuron Explorer each ATen operation follows the same lifecycle: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running, and a dependency chain viewer traces one op across lanes.
insights.speaker: Josh Longenecker
insights.so_what: Lets engineers localize latency to dispatch, scheduling or execution.
insights.quote: Each ATen operation follows the same pattern

insights.claim: In eager mode, naive RMSNorm built from individual PyTorch ops spends 2.355 ms of Neuron device time, with the three aten::mul calls accounting for 1,164.5 microseconds or 49.5%, aten::add 434.6 microseconds, aten::rsqrt 415.0 microseconds and aten::mean 340.8 microseconds.
insights.speaker: Josh Longenecker
insights.so_what: Shows how many small unfused ops dominate device time on this backend.
insights.quote: The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

insights.claim: aten::add triggers a host-to-device copy because the epsilon scalar starts on the CPU, an overhead that appears in the full key_averages() output.
insights.speaker: Josh Longenecker
insights.so_what: Hidden transfers inflate cost of tiny ops and are only visible through profiling.
insights.quote: aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU.

insights.claim: torch.rms_norm lowers to a single fused Neuron kernel (aten::_fused_rms_norm) with 403.3 microseconds of device time and about 48 microseconds of CPU time versus about 125 microseconds for the naive version.
insights.speaker: Josh Longenecker
insights.so_what: Using built-in fused ops is a free performance win on Trainium.
insights.quote: Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel

insights.claim: Compiling the naive RMSNorm with torch.compile(backend='neuron') produces one Torch-Compiled Region and one NEFF with 375.5 microseconds of device time and 98.4 microseconds of CPU time, comparable to the hand-fused torch.rms_norm at 403 microseconds.
insights.speaker: Josh Longenecker
insights.so_what: The compiler discovers fusion automatically, so developers need not rewrite model code to use fused kernels.
insights.quote: the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function

insights.claim: Both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile take about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time because fusion removes gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediates like x_sq and mean_sq.
insights.speaker: Josh Longenecker
insights.so_what: Kernel fusion and avoiding intermediate tensors are the main lever for inference performance on Trainium.
insights.quote: Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions

insights.claim: With TorchDynamo capturing an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowering to ATen ops, the Neuron backend receives the complete graph, fuses operations, optimizes memory access and compiles it into a single NEFF that runs as one hardware dispatch.
insights.speaker: Josh Longenecker
insights.so_what: Explains the compile path that Trainium users depend on for efficiency.
insights.quote: The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

insights.claim: The recommended profiling workflow is to find a hotspot in the key_averages() table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost, and it applies to larger models.
insights.speaker: Josh Longenecker
insights.so_what: A repeatable method for optimizing inference on Trainium.
insights.quote: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost

insights.claim: Part 2 of the series will move to device-level profiling: opening the NEFF, inspecting TensorEngine, VectorEngine and DMA breakdown, and placing the kernel on the roofline to decide if it is compute-bound or memory-bound.
insights.speaker: Josh Longenecker
insights.so_what: Signals upcoming deeper hardware-level content on Trainium engines.
insights.quote: place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound
